title: India's 10-Year Yield Falls to 7.07% as Democrats' Sweep Cuts Oil and US Yields
excerpt: Benchmark Indian bond yields dropped 12 basis points after the US midterm result, as falling crude, a stronger rupee and lower Treasury yields combined — and fund managers say the December RBI review is now the key test.
body:
• India's benchmark 10-year government bond yield fell as much as 12 basis points to 7.07% on Thursday, extending its weekly decline to about 35 basis points after Democrats won both chambers of the US Congress.
  • The US 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.85%, and Brent crude fell about 8.5% to $94.20 a barrel in Asian trade, down nearly 20% this week.
  • The rupee strengthened as much as 0.3% to 94.3250 per dollar, touching a 15-day high as crude fell and foreign inflows picked up.
  • For Indian bond investors, fund managers quoted by Mint say existing long-duration and gilt fund holders gain most when yields fall; new investors are advised not to chase duration after the rally.

Indian government bond yields fell sharply on Thursday as the Democratic Party's sweep of both chambers of the US Congress rippled through global markets, pushing down US Treasury yields and crude oil prices at the same time. According to Bloomberg data cited by Mint, the benchmark Indian yield dropped as much as 12 basis points to 7.07%, while the Nifty 50 surged as much as 2%, taking its weekly gains close to 6% and putting it on course for its best week since 2021.

Where yields stand now

TradingView data published by Mint at 11:50 a.m. put the 10-year government bond yield at 7.090% in India, 4.847% in the United States and 2.760% in Japan, all lower on the day. CNBC-TV18 reported that India's benchmark yield fell to a 40-day low of about 7.1% as crude and US yields declined together, and that the rupee opened at 94.35 per dollar against Wednesday's close of 94.64 before strengthening further.

Why the midterm result moved Indian bonds

Fund managers quoted by Mint pointed to two channels. The first is oil: India imports most of its crude, so cheaper oil means lower imported inflation, a smaller import bill and a stronger rupee, all of which pull bond yields down. The second is the US yield itself. Amit Modani, senior fund manager and lead for fixed income at Shriram AMC, described the US 10-year Treasury yield as effectively the world's benchmark interest rate: when it moves, borrowing costs elsewhere tend to follow. A divided government in Washington makes large tax cuts and new spending harder to pass, which means smaller deficits, less government borrowing and fewer bonds issued — and fewer bonds for sale means higher prices and lower yields.

Nishchay Nath, founder and CEO of BondScanner, said yields are falling as markets reassess two risks — elevated oil prices and US government borrowing — and noted that India's 10-year yield has fallen to around 7.1% from close to 7.5% less than two weeks ago. Anand K. Rathi, co-founder of MIRA Money, added that improved currency sentiment and short-covering in government bonds also contributed to the decline.

What it means for bond and mutual fund investors

Bond prices move inversely to yields, so the fall is good news for existing holders: long-duration and gilt funds gain the most, and their net asset values should have risen over the past few sessions, Modani said. Rathi suggested investors with a lower risk appetite consider short-duration funds, which are less sensitive to interest-rate moves, while those with a longer horizon and higher risk tolerance may consider long-duration funds. Modani's advice was to stay invested, focus on quality and accrual, and avoid chasing duration after this rally.

What could reverse the move

The rally rests heavily on oil. Nath cautioned that the fall in yields reflects expectations of lower oil prices more than any change in actual supply, so yields could move higher again if crude rebounds. The Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate to 5.5% last month and moved to a calibrated tightening stance, making its December policy review the next major local catalyst. Modani expects yields to remain volatile in the near term; Rathi said the direction will depend on oil, domestic inflation, RBI policy, government borrowing and US Treasury yields. Reuters reported that Indian shares were set to open higher on Thursday as crude hit a two-month low, with investors betting the Democrats' victory could hasten an end to the US-Israeli war on Iran.
